records.name: Grass Patch
records.description: A soft patch of regrowing grass. A first step for any bare ground.

records.name: Native Grass Patch
records.description: Deep-rooted native bunchgrass. Food and cover for meadow life.

records.name: Wildflower Patch
records.description: Mixed native wildflowers. Pollinators can spot it from far away.

records.name: Poppy Patch
records.description: California poppies (Eschscholzia californica), a native western wildflower, grown from seed in a watered bed — they close their petals on cloudy days.

records.name: Sunflower Patch
records.description: Tall common sunflowers (Helianthus annuus), a true North American native, left standing so their seed heads feed finches right through the autumn.

records.name: Lupine Patch
records.description: Spires of blue lupine that fix the soil as they bloom.

records.name: Willow Tree
records.description: The preserve's namesake — a graceful willow grown from a watered bed.

records.name: Oak Tree
records.description: An acorn-grown oak. Oaks feed more kinds of caterpillar than any other tree in North America — roughly 500 species — so planting one feeds every insect-eating bird for decades.

records.name: Pine Tree
records.description: A young pine grown from a cone — evergreen shelter in any season.

records.name: Butterfly Flowers
records.description: A mixed bed of native nectar flowers — blazing star, aster and bee balm — planted for adult butterflies. Milkweed is now its own plant; caterpillars need that separately.

records.name: Pollinator Garden
records.description: A dense, season-long banquet for bees and butterflies.

records.name: Shrub
records.description: A young native shrub. Quick cover for anyone passing through — but a meadow is a grassland, and letting shrubs spread across it pushes meadowlarks and other grassland birds out.

records.name: Berry Bush
records.description: A native thimbleberry and wild rose thicket — prickly, as most native brambles are. Songbirds, rabbits and deer all visit. Sow it in a watered bed from seeds and a few berries.

records.name: Small Pond
records.description: A clay-lined pond. Clean drinking water changes everything.

records.name: Woodland Pool
records.description: A shaded forest pool fed by a cold spring. Deer, raccoons, and salamanders all come to drink.

records.name: Fern Spring
records.description: A mossy seep ringed with ferns — damp ground that wakes the whole understory.

records.name: Shallow Water Pool
records.description: A gently sloped pool, safe for small animals to wade and drink. Useful for drinking and bathing — but note that neither salamander in this forest breeds in water, so do not build it for them.

records.name: Log Shelter
records.description: Stacked fallen logs. Small mammals, salamanders, and insects move in fast.

records.name: Hollow Log
records.description: A fallen log carefully opened into a den. Small mammals and foxes love it.

records.name: Rock Pile
records.description: Sun-warmed stones with cool gaps beneath — insects, lizards, and ground beetles approve.

records.name: Fallen Branch Shelter
records.description: A loose brush pile. Humble, but everyone hides in it.

records.name: Bird Perch
records.description: A tall snag for singing and scouting.

records.name: Stepping-Stone Path
records.description: Flat stepping stones that keep your boots off the new growth.

records.name: Gravel Path
records.description: Crunchy gravel underfoot — keeps boots off the new growth.

records.name: Plank Path
records.description: Weathered boardwalk planks, kind to soft ground.

records.name: Flagstone Path
records.description: Broad flat stones set into the earth.

records.name: Mossy Path
records.description: Old stones wearing soft green moss — they keep boots off the wet ground without compacting it.

records.name: Wooden Bridge
records.description: A sturdy plank bridge — place it over a pond or wet swale so boots stay off the soft ground.

records.name: Wooden Fence
records.description: A low rail fence that marks quiet zones for recovering ground.

records.name: Nesting Tree
records.description: A fast-growing native tree planted for squirrels, owls, and nuthatches.

records.name: Standing Deadwood
records.description: A safely anchored dead snag. The bigger around it is, the more it is worth — a small woodpecker needs a stub, a pileated needs a trunk, and everything that nests in their old holes needs the pileated to have found one.

records.name: Mushroom Log
records.description: A damp, mossy log seeded with fungi. The fungus is doing the real work — it digests the wood, which is what turns a dead log into food, soil and shelter for everything else.

records.name: Reed Bed
records.description: Dense replanted reeds — nursery for frogs, dragonflies, and blackbirds.

records.name: Mud Bank
records.description: A shaped soft bank for burrowing and basking. Requires the restoration shovel.

records.name: Nesting Platform
records.description: A raised, quiet platform for open-nesting waterbirds such as ospreys and geese. It is not a substitute for a tree cavity, a bank tunnel or a colony rookery.

records.name: Cattail Stand
records.description: Tall cattails along the water's edge — cover for nesting marsh birds and shade for the shallows.

records.name: Marsh Log
records.description: A half-sunken log. Turtles haul out on top to bask, crayfish and young fish shelter in the dark gaps beneath, and an otter can slip under it out of sight.

records.name: Lily Pool
records.description: Still, clean water blanketed with lily pads — a hatchery for dragonflies and frogs.

records.name: Burrow Mound
records.description: A starter burrow bank for diggers. Requires the restoration shovel.

records.name: Cactus Patch
records.description: Transplanted native pad and barrel cactus. Fruit, moisture and a spiny fortress in one — but no cactus this short can hold a nest cavity.

records.name: Desert Brush
records.description: A mixed stand of bursage and brittlebush — the low scrub that fills the gaps between the bigger shrubs.

records.name: Shaded Rock Shelter
records.description: Stacked slabs with a cool dark gap — shelter from the midday sun.

records.name: Alpine Wildflower Patch
records.description: Tough little high-country forbs — the nectar, seed and grazing layer that pikas, marmots, bees and butterflies all live off. Forage, not shelter.

records.name: Snowmelt Pool
records.description: A stone-lined pool that catches cold, clean snowmelt. Keep it fishless — high alpine waters were naturally without fish, and stocked trout are the biggest single cause of alpine amphibian decline.

records.name: Tidepool
records.description: A restored rocky pool that holds a pocket of the sea between tides — home to crabs, anemones and hermit crabs, but only ever a pocket.

records.name: American Dunegrass
records.description: Native American dunegrass (Leymus mollis), which holds blowing sand in open, patchy clumps rather than a dense wall.

records.name: Driftwood Shelter
records.description: Weathered driftwood stacked into beach shelter.

records.name: Kelp Wrack
records.description: A protected line of washed-up kelp left where the tide dropped it. Beach hoppers shred it after dark, and the birds of the tide line come for the hoppers — groom the wrack away and the beach food web goes with it.

records.name: Coastal Nesting Area
records.description: A general roped-off quiet stretch of upper beach. For specific species build the right closure instead: a Plover Scrape Closure, Seal Haul-Out Rocks or an Offshore Nesting Island.

records.name: Coral Garden
records.description: DEPRECATED — do not offer in this biome. There are no shallow reef-building corals in the temperate northeast Pacific; reef corals need water around 23-25 C and this coast runs 11-21 C. Replaced by the Kelp Forest object.

records.name: Sea Glass Lantern
records.description: Beach-found glass set into a driftwood frame — it throws soft sea-green light at dusk.

records.name: Tide Chime
records.description: Shells and sea glass strung on driftwood that ring softly in the onshore breeze.

records.name: Pearl Display
records.description: A polished shell cradle for beachcombed treasures. Note: there is no natural pearl fishery on this coast, and taking live shellfish for pearls is not restoration — display only what the tide gave up.

records.name: Sea Glass Path
records.description: Tumbled sea glass pressed into the sand — a glittering walkway that keeps boots off the dunes.

records.name: Small Chest
records.description: A woven-and-wood chest. Holds 120 materials. Anything stored here feeds crafting from anywhere.

records.name: Medium Chest
records.description: A sturdier chest. Holds 250 materials.

records.name: Field Journal Stand
records.description: A little lectern for your field journal — read it anywhere you place one.

records.name: Potted Flowers
records.description: A clay pot of meadow flowers to brighten your camp.

records.name: Wetland Restoration Kit
records.description: Liners, filters, and channel tools — everything needed to re-water the wetland. Crafting it helps unlock Rushwater Wetland.

records.name: Migration Path Marker
records.description: Cairns and markers that restore a safe migration path through the heights. Crafting it helps unlock Pelican Shore.

records.name: Forest Restoration Kit
records.description: Seed mixes, fiber twine, and trail tools to open the overgrown forest path. Crafting it helps unlock Old Hollow Forest.

records.name: Scrubland Restoration Kit
records.description: Sediment sleds and hardy cuttings to carry restoration into the dry scrubland. Crafting it helps unlock Redstone Scrubland.

records.name: Alpine Restoration Kit
records.description: Shade cloth, water caches, and climbing gear for the high country. Crafting it helps unlock Graywind Heights.

records.name: Stone Lantern
records.description: A little stone lantern with a warm glow to light the path.

records.name: Wooden Bench
records.description: A weathered bench — a quiet place to sit and watch the wildlife.

records.name: Garden Arch
records.description: A flowering arch that frames a path. Pretty, and pollinators will visit the flowers — but it is a garden feature, not forest habitat, and no species here depends on one.

records.name: Bird Bath
records.description: Fresh water for songbirds to drink and bathe.

records.name: Trail Signpost
records.description: A hand-painted signpost to guide visitors through the preserve.

records.name: Planter Box
records.description: A timber box planted with desert natives — brittlebush, penstemon and globemallow rather than garden flowers.

records.name: Gazebo
records.description: A roofed open-air pavilion — a charming centerpiece and a shady spot to watch the preserve.

records.name: Native Clover Patch
records.description: Springbank clover (Trifolium wormskioldii), a native western clover — nectar for bees and forage for rabbits, and it feeds nitrogen back into the soil.

records.name: Brush Pile
records.description: A loose pile of branches — cover for small mammals and ground birds.

records.name: Fern Grove
records.description: Shady arching ferns that carpet the forest floor.

records.name: Tree Stump
records.description: A mossy old stump riddled with cavities for dens and grubs.

records.name: Sedge Tussock
records.description: Clumped sedges along the shallows — nesting cover for marsh birds.

records.name: Alder Snag
records.description: A standing dead alder drowned by rising water, its trunk riddled with old cavities — a nest hole above the surface for cavity-nesting ducks and a fishing perch for everyone else.

records.name: Agave Rosette
records.description: A spiny rosette whose tall bloom feeds desert pollinators.

records.name: Ocotillo
records.description: Whip-like stalks with crimson tips — cover and nectar in the open flats.

records.name: Heather Mat
records.description: A low alpine mat of heather blossoms above the talus.

records.name: Krummholz Pine
records.description: A wind-sculpted dwarf pine — rare shelter at the tree line.

records.name: Eelgrass Bed
records.description: Swaying eelgrass (Zostera marina) in a sheltered bay — nursery for young fish and the winter pasture that brant geese migrate for.

records.name: Oyster Bed
records.description: A restored reef of native Olympia oysters (Ostrea lurida) — the Pacific coast's own oyster and a real restoration target, not the introduced Pacific oyster.

records.name: Blanketflower Patch
records.description: Blanketflower (Gaillardia aristata), a native western daisy with red-and-gold rays that blooms all summer for bees and butterflies.

records.name: Penstemon Spires
records.description: Tall blue-purple spires of Rocky Mountain penstemon (Penstemon strictus) — a native bumblebee favourite with the same shape as foxglove.

records.name: Mushroom Ring
records.description: A fairy ring of woodland mushrooms in the leaf litter.

records.name: Birch Tree
records.description: A slender white-barked birch grown from a watered bed.

records.name: Marsh Marigold
records.description: Golden marsh marigolds ringing the seepy shallows in spring — the first nectar in the marsh, and a reliable sign of the wet-meadow edge that frogs depend on.

records.name: Bulrush
records.description: Stately bulrushes with brown velvet heads along the bank.

records.name: Prickly Pear
records.description: Pad cactus with sweet fruit and bright blooms.

records.name: Desert Marigold
records.description: Drought-tough marigolds that glow against the sand.

records.name: Alpine Gentian
records.description: Vivid blue alpine gentians, low against the wind.

records.name: Moss Cushion
records.description: A springy cushion of moss campion and alpine avens, warm and damp inside. Seedlings and small invertebrates shelter within the cushion itself.

records.name: Sea Thrift
records.description: Pink sea-thrift pompoms that thrive in salt spray.

records.name: Beach Shrub
records.description: A salt-hardy grey-green coastal scrub of the back dune and bluff — nest cover for gulls on offshore rock and for hummingbirds behind the beach.

records.name: Nectar Feeder
records.description: A sugar-water feeder. Pretty, and fun to watch — but hummingbirds need real flowers to survive, so treat this as decoration, not habitat.

records.name: Crystal Cairn
records.description: A cracked geode set on stacked stones — a glittering desert landmark.

records.name: Sun Totem
records.description: A carved sandstone totem crowned with a desert crystal.

records.name: Palo Verde Tree
records.description: The green-barked desert tree — rare shade and yellow blooms for the scrubland.

records.name: Shore Pine
records.description: A salt-bent pine that anchors the back dunes and shelters shorebirds.

records.name: Bald Cypress
records.description: A towering swamp cypress with a flared, knee-rooted base — a southeastern bottomland tree, planted here as an ornamental. It is outside its natural range in a northern emergent marsh.

records.name: Water Tupelo
records.description: A round-crowned wetland tree whose swollen base stands in the water — a southeastern bottomland species, planted here as an ornamental and outside its natural range.

records.name: Mesquite
records.description: A low, spreading desert tree — airy shade and seed pods for the scrubland.

records.name: Desert Ironwood
records.description: A dense, slow-growing ironwood — a vital nurse tree in the open desert.

records.name: Subalpine Fir
records.description: A slender spire fir that shrugs off the high-country snow.

records.name: Quaking Aspen
records.description: White-barked aspen whose golden leaves shiver in the wind. It grows in sheltered subalpine basins well below the tundra, never above treeline.

records.name: Monterey Cypress
records.description: A wind-flattened coastal cypress sculpted by the sea breeze — planted here, not native: wild Monterey cypress survives in only two relict groves on the Monterey Peninsula.

records.name: Coast Live Oak
records.description: A broad evergreen oak that anchors the back shore with deep shade.

records.name: Campfire
records.description: A crackling campfire ringed with stones — the heart of camp.

records.name: String Lights
records.description: A string of warm little lanterns to hang over your camp.

records.name: Pinwheel
records.description: A bright pinwheel that spins in the breeze.

records.name: Birdhouse
records.description: A hand-built birdhouse on a post — charming, even when empty.

records.name: Flower Cart
records.description: A little wooden cart overflowing with cut flowers.

records.name: Hammock
records.description: A woven hammock strung between two posts for lazy afternoons.

records.name: Garden Gnome
records.description: A cheerful little gnome to watch over the garden.

records.name: Wind Chimes
records.description: Driftwood chimes that sing softly when the wind moves through.

records.name: Sundial
records.description: A carved stone sundial for telling time the slow way.

records.name: Stone Cairn
records.description: A balanced stack of smooth stones marking a quiet spot.

records.name: Picnic Blanket
records.description: A checked blanket spread out for a sunny picnic.

records.name: Flower Pot Row
records.description: A tidy row of terracotta pots brimming with blooms.

records.name: Insect Hotel
records.description: A stack of hollow and pithy stems and beetle-bored bark. Solitary bees nest one egg to a cell inside the tubes — a leafcutter bee seals each cell with a disc she has cut from a leaf.

records.name: Dry Stone Wall
records.description: A low wall of stacked stones with cool, shady gaps for small creatures.

records.name: Bat Box
records.description: A tall, narrow roost box where bats shelter through the day.

records.name: Leaf Litter Pile
records.description: A mound of damp leaves and moss alive with forest-floor life.

records.name: Duck Nest Box
records.description: A raised wooden box where cavity-nesting waterfowl raise their young.

records.name: Basking Log
records.description: A half-submerged log angled up into the sun. A turtle cannot digest its food until it has warmed up, so a log out of the water is not decoration — it is a feeding requirement.

records.name: Rock Crevice
records.description: Stacked slabs leaving shady cracks where reptiles shelter from the heat.

records.name: Dew Basin
records.description: A shallow clay basin that catches dew and rain — precious desert water.

records.name: Talus Pile
records.description: A jumble of broken rock — the burrows and runways pikas love.

records.name: Nest Shelf
records.description: A sheltered rock ledge lined with moss for high-country nesters.

records.name: Driftwood Pile
records.description: A tangle of sun-bleached driftwood that shelters shore life.

records.name: Nesting Bluff
records.description: A built-up sandy bank with ledges for cliff-nesting seabirds.

records.name: Pika Haypile
records.description: A stockpile of dried grasses and flowers, cured the way pikas hoard hay for the long winter.

records.name: Lichen Boulder
records.description: A weathered boulder crusted with map lichen. It grows roughly a millimetre every ten years, quietly crumbling the rock into the first grains of alpine soil.

records.name: Scree Slope
records.description: A shifting apron of shattered rock, laced with the runways and hideaways of the high country.

records.name: Snowbank Roost
records.description: A packed drift of late-lying snow. A white-tailed ptarmigan burrows into snow like this to roost out of the wind and cold.

records.name: Whitebark Seed Cache
records.description: A hidden larder of whitebark pine nuts — the seed bank nutcrackers and grosbeaks live by.

records.name: Juniper Thicket
records.description: A low, hardy juniper heavy with frosted berries — cover and winter food where little else grows.

records.name: Cliff Nest Niche
records.description: A sheltered cleft in the cliff face, mossed and tucked away for high-country nesters.

records.name: Crystal Snowmelt Spring
records.description: An ice-cold spring welling up through quartz — the purest, coldest water in the heights.

records.name: Summit Prayer Flags
records.description: A bright line of weatherworn flags strung between cairns, snapping in the alpine wind.

records.name: Quartz Lantern
records.description: A stone lantern set with a glowing shard of quartz that holds the last of the daylight.

records.name: Obsidian Totem
records.description: A polished column of volcanic glass that catches the high light like dark, still water.

records.name: Large Chest
records.description: A big iron-banded storage chest. Holds 500 materials — your main stockpile.

records.name: Woven Rug
records.description: A soft woven rug to warm the floor of your home.

records.name: Little Table
records.description: A small wooden table with a sprig of flowers.

records.name: Cozy Bed
records.description: A comfortable bed for resting between restoration days.

records.name: Bookshelf
records.description: A shelf of field guides and well-thumbed nature books.

records.name: Cozy Armchair
records.description: A plush armchair to sink into after a long day's restoring.

records.name: Stone Fireplace
records.description: A crackling stone hearth that warms the whole room.

records.name: Floor Lamp
records.description: A soft floor lamp for cozy evenings indoors.

records.name: House Plant
records.description: A leafy potted plant to bring a little of the meadow inside.

records.name: Framed Landscape
records.description: A framed painting of the preserve at its finest.

records.name: Sleeping Bag
records.description: A simple sleeping bag — just the thing for a cozy night in the tent.

records.name: Floor Cushions
records.description: A pile of soft floor cushions for lounging.

records.name: Wooden Stool
records.description: A simple cushioned stool.

records.name: Mushroom Shelf
records.description: A little shelf dotted with woodland mushrooms.

records.name: Reed Floor Mat
records.description: A woven reed mat from the marsh.

records.name: Potted Cactus
records.description: A hardy little cactus in a clay pot.

records.name: Driftwood Shelf
records.description: A shelf of weathered driftwood with beach finds.

records.name: Wall Clock
records.description: A handsome wall clock — a house needs one.

records.name: Wooden Dresser
records.description: A sturdy chest of drawers.

records.name: Woolly Rug
records.description: A thick, warm rug for cold mountain nights.

records.name: Antler Chandelier
records.description: A grand candle chandelier — fit for a lodge.

records.name: Aquarium
records.description: A glass tank of darting little fish.

records.name: Stargazing Telescope
records.description: A brass telescope for the clear mountain sky.

records.name: Rain Basin
records.description: A carved stone bowl that catches rainwater — a drinking spot for visiting wildlife.

records.name: Dewlit Lantern
records.description: Decoration. A glass globe of glowing morning dew that throws a soft green light — invented, not habitat.

records.name: Sunstone Cairn
records.description: Decoration. A stack of sun-baked stones that hold the day's warmth into the cool evening — pretty, but no meadow animal needs one.

records.name: Frostflower Planter
records.description: Decoration. A planter of imaginary pale ice-blooms — a made-up flower, not a plant you could grow.

records.name: Stormglass Lantern
records.description: A shard of lightning-fused glass that flickers with a cold inner light.

records.name: Frostflower Vase
records.description: A glass vase of ice-blooms for the windowsill — they never wilt.

records.name: Stormglass Chandelier
records.description: A hanging cluster of lightning-glass shards that scatters cool light across the room.

records.name: Marsh Boardwalk
records.description: A raised plank walkway. No animal needs one — it exists so that you don't: every footstep off it compacts mud, crushes stems and opens a path a predator can follow to a nest.

records.name: Heron Rookery
records.description: A stand of tall snags and crowns carrying a dozen bulky stick nests. A rookery is a colony, not a single nest — great blue herons hunt alone but will only breed alongside each other.

records.name: Dragonfly Pond
records.description: A clear pool ringed with reeds — open water where dragonfly nymphs hunt below the surface and climb the stems to emerge as adults, and where frogs lay their eggs.

records.name: Trail Tent
records.description: A snug canvas tent you can step inside and decorate — a little home base away from home. Pitch one in each wild biome beyond the meadow.

records.name: Headlamp
records.description: A hand-wound lamp on a woven strap. Once crafted it's yours for good — after dusk, a warm beam lights the ground around you wherever you roam.

records.name: Field Binoculars
records.description: Hand-ground lenses in a woven grip. Once crafted they're yours for good — animals you haven't recorded in your journal yet catch the light with a soft glint.

records.name: Hiking Boots
records.description: Sturdy boots cobbled from tough forest bark, springy moss, and woven wetland reeds. Once crafted they're yours for good — wear them to roam the preserve a little faster.

records.name: Fellfield Gravel
records.description: Wind-scoured gravel that freezes, heaves and re-sorts itself every spring, held together by thin crusts of lichen. It looks like nothing, and it is the only ground a cushion plant will take.

records.name: Alpine Turf Mat
records.description: A knitted mat of sedge, alpine avens and cushion plants over dark alpine soil. Turf like this takes decades to close over bare ground, and one summer of boot traffic to open it up again.

records.name: Snowmelt Litter Mat
records.description: A sodden mat of last year's stems and leaves, released as the snowpack pulls back. Almost all of the alpine's decomposition happens in these few damp weeks.

records.name: Rotting Conifer Log
records.description: A well-rotted subalpine fir log lying where the drifts pile deepest, soft enough to push a finger into. Dead wood is habitat, not mess.

records.name: Escape Cliff
records.description: A near-vertical band of broken cliff where a bighorn can climb out of a predator's reach in seconds. Sheep will not graze a slope they cannot escape from.

records.name: Willow Basin Thicket
records.description: Planeleaf and snow willow filling a sheltered basin. Willow buds and twigs are almost the entire winter diet of a white-tailed ptarmigan, and the best browse a snowshoe hare or a mule deer will find this high.

records.name: Boulder Burrow Den
records.description: A deep, many-chambered burrow tunnelled under a boulder, well below the frost line. A marmot spends about eight months of the year asleep down here.

records.name: Inherited Earth Den
records.description: An old marmot burrow, widened and taken over. Red foxes rarely dig their own den if somebody else has already done the digging.

records.name: Stonecrop Patch
records.description: Lance-leaved stonecrop wedged into gravel and rock cracks. It is the only plant a Rocky Mountain Parnassian caterpillar will eat.

records.name: Bumble Bee Nest Burrow
records.description: An abandoned rodent tunnel packed with dry grass. An alpine bumble bee queen cannot dig — she has to find a hole somebody else left behind.

records.name: Chipmunk Burrow Larder
records.description: A shallow tunnel under a slab, packed with seed heads. A least chipmunk does not fatten up for winter — it sleeps in short stretches and wakes to eat from its own larder.

records.name: Whitebark Pine
records.description: A whitebark pine grown from a seed a nutcracker buried and never came back for. Its cones do not open on their own, so without the bird the tree cannot spread at all.

records.name: Beetle-Killed Snag
records.description: A big standing dead fir, its wood loosened by bark beetles. The larvae feed the birds, and the softened trunk is where woodpeckers cut the holes everything else moves into.

records.name: Old Woodpecker Cavity
records.description: A nest hole chiselled out of a dead trunk seasons ago and left behind. Bluebirds cannot cut one and chickadees can only manage it where the wood is already rotten — every cavity they use was made by a woodpecker first.

records.name: Snowfield Debris Line
records.description: The dark seam of wind-carried seeds, pollen and chilled insects stranded on a shrinking snowfield — a free meal delivered uphill by the wind, and one of the odd ways an alpine slope is fed from below.

records.name: Toad Upland Burrow
records.description: A borrowed rodent tunnel in damp ground above a breeding pool. A boreal toad spends September to May down one of these, below the frost and above the water table.

records.name: Treeline Log Den
records.description: A hollow log at the edge of the last trees, buried by drifts all winter. A marten dens here and hunts the tunnels under the snowpack.

records.name: Fur-Lined Prey Den
records.description: A stolen rodent burrow, relined with the fur of the animal that dug it. Ermines take over their prey's homes rather than build their own.

records.name: Cliff Eyrie
records.description: A bulky stick eyrie on a sheer ledge, added to year after year until the same pair has used it for decades.

records.name: Ledge Natal Den
records.description: A dry overhang deep in broken cliff, screened by fallen rock, where a female mountain lion hides her kittens through their first two months.

records.name: Krummholz Bed Hollow
records.description: A shaded, wind-broken hollow scraped out under the krummholz, where a mule deer beds down through the middle of the day.

records.name: Kelp Holdfast Reef
records.description: Clean rock on the shallow seafloor for kelp holdfasts to grip. Kelp is not rooted in sand — without hard bottom the whole forest washes away.

records.name: Upwelling Current
records.description: Cold, nutrient-rich water rising from the deep along the shore. It is the fertiliser of this whole coast: kelp, plankton, anchovies and filter feeders all run on it.

records.name: Coralline Turf
records.description: Pink, branching coralline and red algae turf on low-zone rock. Surfgrass seeds carry bristly arms that hook onto these branches — no turf, no surfgrass.

records.name: Low-Tide Rock Bench
records.description: A broad shelf of bedrock uncovered only at the lowest tides — the richest strip of the shore, and the one that is underwater most of the time.

records.name: Urchin Pit
records.description: Rounded hollows ground into solid rock by urchins' teeth and spines. An urchin may sit in the same pit for years, catching drift kelp as it sweeps past.

records.name: Kelp Forest
records.description: Living giant kelp rising from the seafloor to a golden canopy at the surface — food, nursery and shelter for the whole coast, and the thing otters wrap up in to sleep.

records.name: Surfgrass Bed
records.description: A green meadow of Torrey's surfgrass streaming in the surge on low-zone rock, packed with small invertebrates and young fish.

records.name: Nearshore Spawning Shallows
records.description: Quiet plankton-rich water just off the surf line where anchovy schools spawn and their eggs drift near the surface.

records.name: Open Sand Beach
records.description: Wide, flat, unplanted sand above the tide. Bare open sand is habitat in its own right here — for hoppers below the surface and for the birds that need a clear line of sight.

records.name: Empty Shell Drift
records.description: A pocket of empty snail shells caught in a rock hollow. Hermit crabs carry a borrowed shell their whole lives, and a shore with no spare shells holds no hermit crabs.

records.name: Subtidal Rubble Flat
records.description: Loose cobble and broken rock just below the tide, where dead material collects and the shallow-water cleanup crew works.

records.name: Surge-Swept Rock Face
records.description: Open rock taking the full weight of the swell. Punishing to stand on, perfect to filter from — the water never stops moving past.

records.name: Barnacle Crust
records.description: A white crust of acorn barnacles across the upper rock. It feeds turnstones and sea stars, and its rough shells are where mussel larvae prefer to settle.

records.name: Sheltered Sand-Gravel Flat
records.description: Stable mixed sand and gravel in the lee of a headland — firm enough to burrow into and calm enough to stay put, which is what a buried clam needs.

records.name: Amphipod and Mysid Bed
records.description: Soft sediment and kelp-edge water thick with tube-building amphipods and swarming mysid shrimp — the small crustaceans a gray whale actually eats.

records.name: Sheltered Cobble Field
records.description: Loose stones on a shore the surf does not reach hard. The habitat is the damp underside — lift one and the shore crabs run.

records.name: Splash-Zone Crevice
records.description: Dry-looking cracks in rock the waves only reach as spray. The highest tier of shore life lives here — animals that breathe air and only visit the sea.

records.name: Shell-Dropping Rock
records.description: A flat hard-topped boulder, scattered with cracked shells. Gulls carry clams and crabs up over it and let go — and come back to the same rock all season.

records.name: Swash-Zone Runnel
records.description: The wet, sliding strip where each wave runs out and drains back, turning over mole crabs and amphipods with every surge.

records.name: Plover Scrape Closure
records.description: A roped-off stretch of bare, open, unvegetated sand with symbolic fencing and signs. The nest is only a scrape — what protects it is that nobody walks through.

records.name: High-Tide Roost
records.description: A raised rock or islet that stays dry at high water. Shorebirds cannot feed while the tide is in, so somewhere safe to stand and wait is as necessary as food.

records.name: Dune Manzanita
records.description: Low sandmat manzanita (Arctostaphylos pumila), a coastal dune shrub that flowers in midwinter — nectar exactly when Anna's Hummingbird is already nesting.

records.name: Mussel Bed
records.description: A dense band of California mussels layered across mid-zone rock. It is food for half the shore and, in the gaps between shells, home to hundreds of smaller animals.

records.name: Mussel Bed Lower Margin
records.description: The sharp lower edge of the mussel bed, with open rock below it. That edge is not drawn by the tide — it is drawn by sea stars eating upward, and it moves down the rock when they disappear.

records.name: Sunlit Surge Pool
records.description: A deep pool flushed by every wave and open to the sky — surge to deliver food from the rocks above, sunlight for the algae living inside its anemones.

records.name: Shell-Lined Rock Scrape
records.description: A hand-sized hollow on bare rock just above the highest waves, lined with shell chips and pebbles the birds carry up themselves.

records.name: Offshore Nesting Island
records.description: A rock stack or islet offshore, out of reach of foxes, dogs and footpaths. California brown pelicans nest on offshore islands and nowhere else — no island, no colony.

records.name: Sandbar Roost
records.description: A low sandbar that dries out between tides — somewhere for pelicans, gulls and geese to stand, preen and digest without being disturbed.

records.name: Seal Haul-Out Rocks
records.description: Low rocks and a sand spit with a wide buffer of quiet around them, where seals rest, moult and give birth. Approach one and the seals leave; leave it alone and they stay.

records.name: Sheltered Rafting Cove
records.description: Calm water in the lee of a point, inside the kelp. Sea otters have no blubber — they need still water to groom their fur in and kelp fronds to wrap around themselves while they sleep.

records.name: Creosote Bush
records.description: The dominant shrub of the Sonoran flats, spaced wide apart because its roots take all the water for metres around. Its resinous leaves smell like rain and lose almost none of it.

records.name: Saguaro
records.description: A columnar giant that stores months of rain in its pleated stem. Doves, bats and bees take its flowers, woodpeckers carve its trunk, and everything else eats the fruit.

records.name: Chain-fruit Cholla
records.description: A jointed cactus armoured in barbed spines. Cactus wrens build their football-shaped nests deep inside it, where almost nothing can follow.

records.name: Desert Mistletoe
records.description: A leafless parasitic plant rooted inside mesquite and ironwood branches. Its winter berries are the phainopepla's staple — and the bird plants the next generation.

records.name: Chuparosa
records.description: A soft grey shrub carrying tubular scarlet flowers right through the desert winter — the Costa's Hummingbird's most important natural nectar source.

records.name: Catclaw Acacia
records.description: A low thorny tree of desert washes, hooked all over with curved spines. Quail coveys roost up in it at night and eat the seed pods by day.

records.name: Bush Muhly
records.description: A fine-stemmed native perennial grass that grows up through shrubs for protection. It is the first thing livestock graze away, so its return is a sign the flat is healing.

records.name: Cryptobiotic Soil Crust
records.description: A living skin of cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses knitting the bare soil together. It fixes nitrogen, holds water and blocks weed seedlings — and a single boot or hoof print undoes decades of it.

records.name: Open Bare Ground
records.description: A patch of soft, uncompacted soil deliberately left open between the shrubs. Ground-nesting bees and harvester ants dig here — but only where nothing has packed it hard.

records.name: Harvester Ant Mound
records.description: A gravel-capped Pogonomyrmex colony with a cleared disc around it and seed husks heaped at the edge. The ants harvest seeds, turn tonnes of soil, and are nearly the whole diet of the regal horned lizard.

records.name: Buried Deadwood
records.description: Dead mesquite and creosote stems worked half into the soil. Subterranean termites tunnel up into them from below and never cross the dry open surface.

records.name: Shrub Litter Mound
records.description: Wind-drifted leaves, stems and seed husks caught under a shrub — the surface larder darkling beetles work through at night, and their hiding place by day.

records.name: Termite-Worked Soil
records.description: Soil laced with old termite galleries and sheeted-over litter. This is where most of the desert's dead plants actually go back into the ground, and the tunnels let rain soak in instead of running off.

records.name: Tortoise Burrow
records.description: A long cool den a desert tortoise has dug out and kept open. Burrowing owls, snakes, lizards, rodents and beetles all move in — most of them cannot dig anything like it themselves.

records.name: Caliche Den
records.description: A hollow eroded into a hard caliche bank on a rocky slope. Sonoran desert tortoises den in these and in boulder crevices more often than they dig long burrows of their own.

records.name: Creosote Coppice Mound
records.description: Wind-caught soil heaped around a creosote's base and riddled with kangaroo rat tunnels. Desert iguanas take over these burrows to sit out the hottest hours.

records.name: Seed Larder Burrow
records.description: A shallow burrow under a shrub with side chambers packed full of seeds, its entrances plugged with sand every dawn. The plug traps humid air the kangaroo rat needs as much as the food.

records.name: Deep Sand Burrow
records.description: A spiral shaft driven as much as two and a half metres into loose soil — the giant hairy scorpion's refuge from heat and dryness for most of the year.

records.name: Kit Fox Den
records.description: A cool den with several entrances — nearly always a rodent burrow a kit fox has widened rather than one it dug from scratch. The extra doors are escape routes from coyotes.

records.name: Wash Bank Den
records.description: An earthen den dug into the cut bank of a dry wash, set above the flood line, where a coyote pair raises its pups.

records.name: Snake Den
records.description: A deep rock fissure that stays above freezing all winter. Diamondbacks return to the same den year after year, sometimes for decades, and several may share it.

records.name: Saguaro Boot
records.description: The hard waterproof scar a saguaro grows around a Gila Woodpecker's hole. Months later the woodpecker moves out and an elf owl moves in — the boot outlasts them both.

records.name: Thorn Thicket Nest
records.description: A bulky stick platform wedged a metre or two up inside a thorny shrub — high enough and prickly enough for a roadrunner pair to raise chicks out of a coyote's reach.

records.name: Carrion Ground
records.description: An animal that has died, left where it fell instead of hauled away. Ravens find it within hours, beetles and ants follow, and in a few days its nutrients are back in the soil.

records.name: Saguaro Fruit Fall
records.description: Split crimson saguaro fruit at the height of the June heat, just before the rains. For a few weeks it is the richest food and the wettest drink in the whole desert.

records.name: Cactus Fruit Set
records.description: Prickly pear and cholla hanging heavy with ripe fruit. The crop only sets where cactus bees worked the flowers first — no bees, no fruit, no midsummer water for the animals that live on it.

records.name: Shade Form
records.description: A shallow scrape hollowed out in the shade under a shrub. A jackrabbit lies here through the midday heat with its huge ears up, pouring heat into the air.

records.name: Browse Exclosure
records.description: A low fence around a patch of oak seedlings. In a forest with plenty of deer, browsing kills more young oaks than anything else — inside the fence, acorns get to become trees.

records.name: Nurse Log Seedbed
records.description: A rotting, moss-covered log lying on the forest floor. Hemlock seeds that land on bare leaf litter almost always fail; the ones that land on rotten wood become the next generation of trees.

records.name: Deep Duff Layer
records.description: Years of undisturbed leaf mould, never raked and never driven over, threaded through with tree roots and fungal strands. This is where the forest's fungi actually live.

records.name: Truffle Patch
records.description: Underground fungal tubers clustered on oak and hemlock roots. Nothing shows above ground — a flying squirrel has to smell them out and dig.

records.name: Soft-Rot Snag
records.description: A small dead stub whose wood has gone soft with white rot. A downy woodpecker weighs 27 grams and cannot chisel sound timber — it needs wood the fungi reached first.

records.name: Ant-Riddled Log
records.description: A fallen trunk gone punky with rot and tunnelled through by carpenter ant galleries — a pileated woodpecker's entire winter larder.

records.name: Rotted-Out Log
records.description: A log rotted hollow through the middle. A red-backed salamander lays her eggs in the cavity inside and coils around them until they hatch — as tiny salamanders, never as tadpoles.

records.name: Downy Woodpecker Hole
records.description: A round hole about the width of a thumb, cut by a downy woodpecker and abandoned after one season. Nuthatches and chickadees cannot cut their own and move straight in.

records.name: Pileated Cavity Snag
records.description: A large snag carrying last spring's pileated woodpecker nest hole. The pileated cuts a fresh one every year, and flying squirrels, martens, fishers and bats move into the ones it leaves.

records.name: Flooded Cavity Snag
records.description: A dead trunk standing in shallow water with an old woodpecker hole high in it. Wood duck ducklings jump from the entrance the day after they hatch and bounce off the water below.

records.name: Loose-Bark Snag
records.description: A dying tree whose bark has pulled away from the trunk in loose slabs — porcupine gnawing starts many of them — leaving warm, dry gaps where bats spend the day.

records.name: Leaf Drey
records.description: A ball of leaves and twigs wedged into a high fork — a gray squirrel's summer nest, rebuilt every year and inherited by owls when it is done with it.

records.name: Larder Burrow
records.description: A burrow entrance no wider than a coin, with tunnels running metres underground to a nest chamber and a storage room holding more than a litre of seeds.

records.name: Hemlock Stand
records.description: A close-grown group of hemlocks. The canopy holds the snow off the ground beneath it, the shade keeps the stream cold, and the inner bark carries porcupines and deer through the winter.

records.name: Browse Thicket
records.description: Dense young regrowth in a gap where a big tree came down — every twig within reach of a deer's muzzle, which is exactly why too many deer leave nothing here at all.

records.name: Crayfish Shallows
records.description: A stony, ankle-deep margin where crayfish back under the rocks. A raccoon hunts it entirely by touch, its eyes looking somewhere else the whole time.

records.name: Root-Mass Den
records.description: The dry hollow under the tipped-up root plate of a fallen tree — where a black bear sleeps out the winter and gives birth without properly waking up.

records.name: Earth Den Bank
records.description: A well-drained slope with a den dug into it and several entrances. Foxes enlarge and reuse the same bank for generations rather than digging fresh.

records.name: Snake Hibernaculum
records.description: A deep, rubble-filled crack that stays below the frost line all winter. Gartersnakes travel a long way each autumn to reach one and spend the cold months coiled together by the dozen.

records.name: Broken-Top Chimney Tree
records.description: A big living tree snapped off high and hollowed downward by heart rot, leaving a chimney a foot across. No woodpecker cuts a hole this size — a barred owl has to wait for a tree this old.

records.name: Hollow Denning Tree
records.description: A living tree with a rot-hollowed chamber high in the trunk. A female fisher carries her kits up into one within days of birth, out of reach of everything that hunts on the ground.

records.name: Rocky Den Ledge
records.description: A dry gap under a leaning slab of rock, screened by brush. A bobcat raises kittens somewhere like this and will move them the moment anything comes close.

records.name: Adopted Stick Nest
records.description: A bulky old nest of sticks and leaves left behind by a hawk, a crow or a squirrel. A great horned owl never builds its own — it simply takes one over in the middle of winter.

records.name: Bare Soil Scrape
records.description: A hand-cleared patch of open mineral soil. Bare ground is habitat too: seedlings, ground-nesting insects and plovers all need somewhere that isn't covered.

records.name: Native Thistle Stand
records.description: Wavyleaf thistle (Cirsium undulatum), a native prairie thistle — not one of the invasive European kinds. Deep nectar for bumble bees, seed and nest down for goldfinches.

records.name: Prairie Swale Seedbed
records.description: A shallow damp swale of loosened soil, sown in autumn. Showy milkweed and native forbs germinate here where the ground stays moist into early summer.

records.name: Bunchgrass Sod Plug
records.description: Live plugs of blue grama sod pressed into bare ground — the fastest way to restart shortgrass prairie, because each plug already carries its own roots and soil life.

records.name: Grass Thatch Litter
records.description: A deep mat of dead grass stems, leaves and roots left where they fell. This is the raw material meadow fungi take apart and hand back to the soil as minerals.

records.name: Burial Soil Plot
records.description: Loose, uncompacted, moisture-holding soil, deep enough for a burying beetle pair to drag a mouse-sized carcass under and raise their brood in the chamber below.

records.name: Egg Pod Bank
records.description: A strip of firm, sun-warmed bare soil at the edge of the grass. Female grasshoppers drill into it and leave a frothy pod of eggs to overwinter.

records.name: Vole Runway Network
records.description: Narrow runways clipped through dense grass, linking burrow openings and grass nests. Voles patrol them like little highways, and everything that eats voles learns to watch them.

records.name: Milkweed Rhizome Bed
records.description: A spreading bed of showy milkweed grown from rhizome cuttings. It is the only thing a monarch caterpillar can eat, and one bed slowly becomes a patch.

records.name: Nesting Tussock
records.description: A dense unmown grass tussock over an abandoned rodent hole — warm, fur-lined and hidden, which is exactly what a bumble bee queen looks for in spring.

records.name: Brush Form Hollow
records.description: A shallow scrape under low brush — the resting 'form' a cottontail uses instead of digging.

records.name: Serviceberry Browse Thicket
records.description: Saskatoon serviceberry (Amelanchier alnifolia), a native western shrub whose twigs and buds are prime winter browse for mule deer — and whose berries feed birds in late summer.

records.name: Milkweed Aphid Colony
records.description: Bright oleander aphids clustered on milkweed stems. Not a problem to be sprayed — this is the food supply a lady beetle's whole life cycle is built on.

records.name: Wet Meadow Sedge Clump
records.description: A clump of native sedges in a damp low corner of the meadow. Song sparrows hide their ground nests deep inside it, where nothing can see in.

records.name: Burrow Town
records.description: A multi-entrance ground squirrel burrow system dug into deep open soil. Long after the squirrels move on, bumble bee queens, gartersnakes and foxes move in.

records.name: Standing Stem Ootheca
records.description: Stiff dead forb stems left standing through the winter, with a mantis's hardened foam egg case glued to one of them. Cut the stems in autumn and you cut next year's mantises.

records.name: Pebble Nest Scrape
records.description: A bare hollow scratched into open gravelly ground and lined with pebbles. A killdeer nest hidden in plain sight — the eggs look exactly like the stones around them.

records.name: Domed Grass Nest
records.description: A grass-roofed nest cup woven into deep bunchgrass, with a covered runway leading in. Only a real expanse of native grass is tall and thick enough to hide one.

records.name: Bluebird Nest Box
records.description: A nest box with a 1½-inch hole and a predator guard, on a smooth pole facing the open grass. Bluebirds cannot cut their own hole, and boxes like this are why they recovered.

records.name: Snake Hibernaculum
records.description: A rock-and-soil chamber dug below the frost line, often started from an old rodent burrow. Dozens of gartersnakes coil together in one of these to survive the winter.

records.name: Hedgerow Ambush Lane
records.description: A dense line of native shrubs and small trees along the meadow edge. A Cooper's Hawk flies flat out through cover like this to ambush songbirds on the far side.

records.name: Deep Loam Soil Bank
records.description: A bank of deep, stone-free, uncompacted loam. A badger has to be able to dig faster than a ground squirrel can run, and it can only do that in soil like this.

records.name: Earthen Fox Den
records.description: A south-facing bank widened out into a natal den with several exits — usually an old ground squirrel or badger burrow a vixen has enlarged rather than dug from scratch.

records.name: Crown Stick Eyrie
records.description: A bulky platform of sticks wedged into the crown of the tallest tree, with a clear view over open grass. A Red-tailed Hawk builds it — and something bigger inherits it.

records.name: Abandoned Stick Nest
records.description: Last season's hawk nest, weathered and empty. Great Horned Owls never build their own, so one of these standing empty in midwinter is the difference between owls and no owls.

records.name: Sunlit Mudflat
records.description: A bare shelf of wet, sun-warmed mud at the water's edge. Cattail seed is tiny and needs light and open ground to germinate — it will not sprout in shade or under standing water.

records.name: Clearwater Shallows
records.description: Slow water with the silt settled out of it, so sunlight reaches the bottom. Submerged plants live on that light — which is why clear water and underwater meadows always arrive together.

records.name: Litter Drift
records.description: A submerged raft of dead cattail and sedge leaves, softening under a fur of fungi and bacteria. More energy moves through a marsh this way — as dead plants — than through anything eaten alive.

records.name: Crayfish Burrow Bank
records.description: A saturated clay bank riddled with finger-wide tunnels. Crayfish back into them to moult in safety and to wait out low water when the marsh draws down in late summer.

records.name: Submerged Spawning Slab
records.description: A flat stone or plank lying just below the surface. Male fathead minnows scrub the underside clean, and the females stick their eggs to that ceiling for him to guard.

records.name: Stable Silt Shoal
records.description: A broad shelf of settled silt and fine sand in water slow enough that it stays put. A mussel buries itself here and may filter the same patch of water for thirty years.

records.name: Cattail Root Shallows
records.description: Shallow water over a dense mat of cattail rootstocks. This is a muskrat's winter larder — it dives under the ice and digs up the starchy roots when everything above is frozen.

records.name: Flooded Reed Clump
records.description: A tight stand of cattail and reed stems standing in ankle-deep water. A blackbird winds its nest around several upright stems, and the water underneath is what keeps the mink out.

records.name: Winter Litter Mound
records.description: A deep pile of damp leaves, loose bark and old stems on dry ground beside the marsh. A chorus frog crawls in, freezes almost solid for the winter, and thaws out alive in spring.

records.name: Fishless Vernal Pool
records.description: A shallow, separate pool that fills with snowmelt and dries out by late summer. Drying is the point: it keeps fish out, and salamander larvae can only survive where no fish can.

records.name: Wet Meadow Margin
records.description: A band of damp, grassy meadow between the marsh and dry land. Leopard frogs spend the whole summer hunting out here, well away from open water — lose this band and you lose the frogs.

records.name: Sandy Nest Bank
records.description: A warm, well-drained rise of sand and fine gravel above the waterline. Female snapping turtles walk overland to dig their nests here — and turtle populations are limited by nest banks, not by adults.

records.name: Crane Nest Mound
records.description: A broad heap of piled marsh plants standing in open shallow water. A crane pair builds it up above the waterline so the two eggs stay dry and anything approaching has to wade.

records.name: Hidden Reed Platform
records.description: A low platform of living reeds bent down and woven together deep inside a dense stand, barely a hand's width above the water. A bittern will not nest anywhere it can be seen.

records.name: Cut Bank Burrow
records.description: A bare, vertical earth bank rising straight out of the water, soft enough to tunnel a metre back into. Kingfishers dig their own nest tunnels here and use no other kind of nest.

records.name: Overwater Thicket
records.description: Low willow and alder leaning right out over the water at the edge of a beaver pond. A green heron builds a loose stick nest on a branch above the surface and fishes from the shade below.

records.name: Old Muskrat Bank Den
records.description: A muskrat's abandoned bank burrow, its entrance under water. Mink hardly ever dig their own — they move into one a muskrat made, so the muskrat has to come back first.

records.name: Otter Bank Den
records.description: A roomy den in the bank with an underwater entrance, almost always a beaver's old lodge or burrow taken over. Otters are excellent swimmers and poor diggers — they let the beaver do the excavating.

records.name: Beaver Pond
records.description: Deep, permanent water held back behind a stick-and-mud dam, with drowned trees standing in it. It is a different habitat from the open cattail marsh — deeper, more open, and only a beaver can make it.

records.name: Beaver Canal
records.description: A shallow channel a beaver digs to float branches back to its pond. It carries water far out into the marsh and keeps turtles and frogs connected to open water even in a dry summer.
